Juan Li1, Zichong Chen 1,2 , Yuzhong Zhang 3, Itziar Irakulis-Loitxate4, Lucas A. Estrada2, Mengze Li5, Xueying Yu6, Mengyao Liu7, Ge Han 8, Drew C. Pendergrass9,10 & Drew Shindell 10

South Asia is a global methane (CH4) hotspot with strong monsoon-driven seasonality, yet wet-season emissions remain poorly constrained due to persistent cloudiness. Here we quantify dry- and wetseason methane emissions separately over South Asia during 2019–2024 using TROPOMIconstrained analytical inversions. By leveraging satellite observations from downwind regions, we are able to effectively constrain wet-season emissions despite sparse coverage. Anthropogenic sources dominate the regional total, accounting for 77.2% (28.8 Tg a−1; interannual range: 25.3–30.9 Tg a⁻¹), with major contributions from livestock (35.0% (32.9%–36.0%)), rice cultivation (21.8% (20.4%–23.1%)), and waste management (13.8% (12.4%–14.5%)). Six-year mean wet-season emissions (49.9(44.6–53.4) Tg a-1) are nearly twice dry season emissions (28.2(23.8–33.6) Tg a−1), driven by wetlands (5.5×), rice (2.6×), waste management (1.2×), and fossil fuels (1.2×); seasonality in waste and fossil fuels emissions is however missing from current inventories. Furthermore, latest national reports underestimate India’s methane emissions partly by neglecting seasonal variability. Despite much larger wet-season emissions, dry-season livestock and waste, unexpectedly, dominate interannual variability, likely indicating sensitivity to climate anomalies and potential implications for climate-resilient mitigation. South Asia contributed substantially to global methane surge in 2021, but not 2020. Our ﬁndings underpin previously-overlooked mitigation priorities that vary sharply by season.

Methane (CH4) is the second largest anthropogenic greenhouse gas after carbon dioxide, with a radiative forcing of 0.97 W m⁻² and an atmospheric lifetime of ~9 years1,2. Anthropogenic methane emissions arise primarily from livestock, rice cultivation, fossil fuel production (oil, gas, and coal), and waste management, while wetlands represent the dominant natural source. The main sink of atmospheric methane is oxidation by the hydroxyl radical (OH) in the troposphere, with additional minor sinks in soils3–5. After a period of relative stabilization, atmospheric methane concentrations began to increase again after 2006 and surged in 2020 and 2021, with annual growth rates of ~14.9 and ~17.7 ppb, respectively (https://gml.noaa.gov/

ccgg/trends_ch4/, last accessed: June 2026). The drivers of this renewed methane growth remain debated, particularly the relative contributions of different regions and source sectors6–12. South Asia is a major global hotspot of methane emissions13,14, characterized by high population density, intensive agriculture, rapid urbanization, and vast wetlands. According to the Global Carbon Project (GCP), South Asia (including Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka) emits ~12.6% of the global total anthropogenic methane emissions and ~4.8% of global wetland emissions14. A pronounced increase inmethane emissions over South Asia wasfound post-2018,largely

driven by anthropogenic sources, particularly livestock, rice cultivation, and waste management15. Natural wetlands may also contribute to recent increases. For example, a recent study found large emission increases in 2020 and 2021 compared to 2019 over the Ganges ﬂoodplain, a region that overlaps with vast tropical wetlands16. Methane emissions in South Asia are dominated by livestock (including enteric fermentation and manure management), rice cultivation, wetlands, and waste (including landﬁlls and wastewater treatment), collectively contributing 46 Tg a−1 or 79% to the regional total according to the GCP ensemble means14. However, substantial uncertainties persist in methane inventories in this region. Bottom-up estimates vary widely in individual sectors14, with livestock emissions spanning 18–22 Tg a−1, rice 5–12 Tg a−1,waste4–11 Tg a−1,andwetlands3–17 Tg a−1.Thesebottom-up estimates are derived by multiplying activity data by underlying emission factors (EFs), following procedures recommended by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)17. Despite being recognized as a key region with high potential for cost-effective abatement10, such high uncertaintiesmake it difﬁcult to set anemissionbaseline and to interpret the contribution of South Asia to recent global methane surge. Methane emissions in South Asia show pronounced seasonality associated with the South Asian monsoon, introducing an additional source of uncertainty. Indeed, large discrepancies are found between top-down observations and bottom-up inventories, and these discrepancies are larger in summer (~16 Tg a−1) than in spring and autumn (~9 Tg a−1)18. A satellite-based study suggested a substantial upward correction of global methane emissions to current inventories for 2018–2019, with over 45% of the increase attributed to India and Southeast Asia during the summer monsoon19. A recent regional study for 2020 also revealed stronger seasonal contrasts relative to existing inventories, with 70% higher methane emissions during the monsoon months (June–September) but 46% lower emissions during January–May20. This seasonal contrast is likely driven by precipitation-enhanced emissions from rice cultivation21,22, manure management19,23, and waste-related sources24,25, as well as from natural wetlands26,27. Recent studies also highlighted the seasonality in fossil fuel emissions28,29. However, the relative contributions of individual source sectors and their sensitivity to climate during the monsoon period remain poorly understood in South Asia. Top-down emission estimates derived from atmospheric methane observations provide independent validation of bottom-up inventories. These inverse analyses apply an atmospheric transport model to relate emissions to atmospheric concentrations and use the bottom-up inventory as prior information30. Satellite observations in the shortwave infrared (SWIR) provide atmospheric methane measurements, which are valuable for top-down inversions31. The Greenhouse Gases Observing Satellite (GOSAT, 2009–present)32 and the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI, 2018–present)33 both measure atmospheric methane columns globally with short revisit times. GOSAT retrievals are accurate with minimal bias, but are spatially sparse with roughly 250 km spacing. TRO- POMI provides daily, high pixel-resolution (7 × 5.5 km2) global measurements but can be biased by surface albedo, aerosols, cirrus, and striping. To leverage bothdata density and accuracy, Balasus et al.34 developed a blended TROPOMI + GOSAT product using machine learning to correct bias. Using these datasets, studies have used analytical Bayesian inversion methodstoestimateglobalandregionalmethaneemissions27,35–43.However, most of these satellite-based analytical inversions inherently focus on annual-mean optimization, without explicitly resolving the seasonal variability of methane emissions; in many cases, emission seasonality is imposed in the prior knowledge, rather than being constrained by observations, which may lead to biased inversion results due to temporal aggregation44. Here,weapplyaregionalBayesianinversionframeworkthatintegrates TROPOMI observations from the blended TROPOMI + GOSAT product34 with the GEOS-Chem chemical transport model over the 2019–2024 period to quantify methane emissions across South Asia. Here, we deﬁne South Asia as India and Bangladesh, which represent the dominant methane-emitting region within the broader South Asian domain. We

focus on these two countries as their methane emissions are strongly inﬂuenced by the South Asian monsoon system20,45, and account for approximately 77% of anthropogenic methane emissions from South Asia (including Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka)46. By performing separate inversions for dry and wet seasons, we explicitly resolve the seasonal and further interannual variability (IAV) in regional methane emissions. This study aims to investigate the seasonal contrast in methane emissions in South Asia, constrain the region’s contribution to recent global methane growth, and quantify sector-speciﬁc contributions in the dry and wet periods to inform effective, targeted mitigation strategies.

Results We conduct an analytical Bayesian inversion of methane emissions over South Asia (India and Bangladesh) at up to 0.25° × 0.3125° (~25 × 25 km2) for the 2019–2024 period, constrained by TROPOMI observations of dry column methane mole fractions (XCH4)34. Following the South Asian monsoon cycle, we apply the inversions separately to the dry season (NovembertoMay)andwetseason(JunetoOctober)foreachyear,tobetter characterize seasonally varying emissions. This represents a trade-off between resolving emission seasonality and ensuring effective observational constraints. An analytical inversion has the advantage of providing closedform error statistics and information content as part of the solution31. We ﬁnd that during the wet season, signals from the downwind regions (the Indian Deserts and the Indus Plain) by satellite observations can be used to constrain methane emissions (see “Methods”, Text S1, Figs. S1 and S2). We quantify posterior emission uncertainties using an ensemble of 108 sensitivity inversions, comprising 9 sensitivity inversions for each of 12 inversion periods (2 seasons × 6 years). The ability to separate sectoral contributions to posterior emissions is evaluated using error correlations in the reduced posterior covariance matrix (Figs. S4 and S5). Prior methane emissions (Fig. S6) are taken from EDGAR v847,48 (livestock, wastewater, landﬁlls, and otheranthropogenicsources),theGlobalRicePaddyInventory(GRPI)22for ricecultivation, the Global Fuel Exploitation Inventory (GFEI v3)49 for fossil fuels including offshore activities, and the Lund-Potsdam-Jena Earth Observation Simulator (LPJ-EOSIM)50 for wetland. The GEOS-Chem chemical transport model (version 13.0.0; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo. 4618180, last accessed: June 2026) is used as the forward model. Further details are provided in the “Methods” section and Supplementary Information.

Evaluation of posterior emission estimates Figure 1 compares the spatial distributions of prior and posterior mean methane emissions in South Asia for the dry and wet seasons averaged over 2019–2024. It also shows diagonal elements of the averaging kernel matrix, which quantiﬁestheextenttowhichTROPOMIsatelliteretrievalsconstrain the posterior emissions independently of the prior (0 = not at all; 1 = fully). Values close to unity indicate strong observational control, arising from dense satellite coverage or large prior emissions. High sensitivities are obtained over major source regions, yielding 148 and 136 degrees of freedom for signal (DOFS) in the dry and wet seasons, respectively, from a 600- element emission state vector parameterized using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM)51 to represent spatial emission patterns (see “Methods”). DOFS represents the number of independent pieces of information provided by the observations to constrain the state vector52. Despite sparse observations during the monsoon due to cloud cover, the wet season retains high DOFS (comparable to that of the dry season) because upwind emissions are transported to downwind regions where satellite observations are denser. Indeed, we design sensitivity tests perturbing emissions at three representative upwind regions, and ﬁnd concentration enhancements from local and downwind observations by TROPOMI (Text S1). Future satellite inversion studies could thus beneﬁt from including downwind regions with observational coverage to improve constraints on emissions in the upwind source regions.

Comparison with TROPOMI XCH4 retrievals shows that prior model simulations overestimate XCH4 in the dry season and underestimate XCH4 in the wet season (Figs. 1h, k and S7). The posterior simulations improve agreement with observations (details for each individual season are provided in Fig. S8), reducing the mean bias from 16.9 (prior) to −0.4 ppb (posterior) in the dry seasons and from −8.6 to −1.0 ppb in the wet seasons, accompanied by marked reductions in root mean square error (RMSE) from 23.1 to 14.1 ppb and from 26.1 to 17.5 ppb (Fig. 1i, l), respectively. The limited improvement in RMSEs reﬂects the observational errors of 14.7 ppb (see “Methods”), which include errors from satellite retrievals, model transport, and representativeness30. We further compare our simulation

with ground-based methane measurements at Nainital, India (NTL, 29.36°N, 79.46°E), obtained using the ﬂask sampling53. The posterior simulation shows improved agreement with these observations, reducing the mean bias from 30.0 (prior) to –9.7 (posterior) ppb and the RMSE from 93.1 (prior) to 71.8 (posterior) ppb (Fig. S9).

Total emissions in the wet season (49.9 (44.6–53.4) Tg a−1) are nearly twice those in the dry season (28.2 (23.8–33.6) Tg a−1). We report dry- and wet-season emissions on an annual basis (Tg a−1) throughout the text to facilitate comparison. Natural emissions are 3.2 (2.4–4.1) Tg a−1 in the dry season and 15.9 (14.6–17.6) Tg a−1 in the wet season, while anthropogenic emissions are 25.0 (20.4–29.5) Tg a−1 and 34.0 (29.8–37.9) Tg a−1, respectively. Figure 2 further shows the seasonal contrast in individual sectors and their contributions to the regional total. As expected, higher wet-season emissions are found in wetlands (5.5× that of dry season) and rice cultivation (2.6×); interestingly, we also ﬁnd larger emissions from waste management (1.2×) and fossil fuels (1.2×) during the wet season. Such seasonal variations in waste and fossil fuel emissions have been recently reported acrossdifferentregionsoftheworld28,29,54–57,yetcurrentemissioninventories generally neglect such seasonality for these sectors (Table S1). By contrast, livestock (1.1×) shows weaker seasonal variability. In terms of sectoral contributions, livestock dominates in the dry season (45.1% (42.9%–47.4%)), followed by rice (17.1% (14.6%–18.4%)), waste (16.5% (13.8%–17.7%)), and wetlands (9.9% (7.2%–12.5%)). In the wet season, emissions are characterized by a much larger wetland contribution (31.1% (27.0%–33.7%)) and rice (25.5% (24.1%–27.1%)), while livestock decreases to 26.9% (25.1%–28.7%) and waste contributes 11.7% (9.2%–12.9%). The inversion uncertainty ranges shown in Fig. 2 vary by sector and are not systematically larger in the wet season, indicating that posterior uncertainty does not scale directly with the number of satellite retrievals. Wetlands and rice cultivation show the largest seasonal amplitudes among all sectors. Higher wet-season emissions in wetlands are associated with warmer temperatures that enhance microbial activity58,59. Increased monsoonal precipitation in South Asia also expands inundated areas and sustains anaerobic soil conditions favorable for methane production16,50

(Fig.S10).Theseasonalpeakinriceemissionsisconsistentwithregionalrice cropping calendars in South Asia21,22. Monsoon-driven inundation overlaps with the active growth stages of dominant rice crops, when enhanced rhizodeposition and root exudates provide organic substrates for methanogenesis in ﬂooded anaerobic soils60,61. Thehigherwet-seasonemissionsinthewastesectorarelikelyrelatedto stimulatedmicrobial methane production and the ineffective waste disposal and treatment as reported inIndia25,62. Opendumps,inparticular,dominate waste disposal in South Asia (75%)63 and emit ~4.8× more methane per unit area than sanitary landﬁlls25. Furthermore, cities in South Asia also lack

wastewater infrastructure; for example, in India, only 28% of wastewater is treated, and less than 8% is reused64. During the monsoon, heavy precipitation degrades landﬁll cover integrity, triggers sewer blockages and overﬂows, and causes surface spreading of untreated wastewater, increasing water residence times and anaerobic conditions, and thereby enhancing methane emissions19,62. Our ﬁnding is consistent with insights derived from the GHGSat satellite survey of landﬁll methane point sources reported by Dogniaux et al.65 (see Text S2). In light of projections of more intense summermonsoons2,ourﬁndingssuggestthatactionsinwastemanagement during wet-season waste emissions in South Asia should be considered in mitigation efforts. Moreover, current inventories use one uniform EF and ignore seasonal variability, leading to an underrepresentation of wet-season emissions. Fossil fuels are assumed to have no seasonality in methane emissions inventories in many previous studies27,49,66,67, but we ﬁnd that, despite their small magnitude and low contribution to total emissions (1.2 (1.0–1.4) Tg a−1; Tables S2 and S3), they show higher emissions in wet seasons(1.2×thatofdryseason).Dangetietal.68observedhigherXCH4over Indian coalﬁelds and power plants in September–October and lower values in the pre-monsoon period (March–May), and argued that it might be associatedwithenergyextractionandconsumption.Indeed,monthlypower demand data from CEIC data (https://www.ceicdata.com/en/india/ electricity-demand-and-supply/electricity-power-peak-demand, last accessed: June 2026) also show higher electricity demand during the wet seasons in India (Figure. S11). Recent studies28,29 have noticed the evident seasonal variation in the U.S., with oil and gas emissions being 20%–50% higher in winterthaninsummeracrossthecentralnorth,centralsouth,andnortheast regions29.DespitedifferinginemissionpeaktimeintheU.S.andSouthAsia, these variations are driven by a common underlying factor: the energy demand and associated methane produced, with increased heating demand during winter in the U.S29. and cooling demand during the wet season (under hot and humid conditions) in South Asia. Livestock emissions are found to have weak seasonal contrasts in our study. Emissions from manure management are expected to show seasonality due to the temperature dependence of microbial activity23,69; however, manure management accounts for a much smaller share than enteric fermentation in South Asia (~7.9% of livestock methane emissions, based on EDGAR)70, resulting in a minor contribution to the overall seasonal variability. The upward corrections are primarily in livestock (+1.7 Tg a⁻¹; interannual range: +0.5 to +2.9 Tg a⁻¹, +4% to +27%), rice (+1.7 Tg a⁻¹; interannual range: +0.9 to +2.1 Tg a⁻¹, +26% to +61%), and waste (+1.6 Tg a⁻¹; interannual range: +0.8 to +2.3 Tg a⁻¹, +30% to +81%). In Bangladesh,ourbestestimateoftheposteriortotalanthropogenicemissions is 4.5 Tg a⁻¹ for 2019–2024 (Fig. 3b and Table S3), which agrees closely with the UNFCCC estimate (4.2 Tg a⁻¹). However, this agreement reﬂects a compensating pattern between our higher estimate in rice (+2.0 Tg a⁻¹; interannual range: +1.7 to +2.4 Tg a⁻¹) and lower estimate in livestock, waste, and fossil fuels (–1.6 Tg a⁻¹ collectively; interannual range: –1.4 to –1.7 Tg a⁻¹). Discrepancies relative to the UNFCCC estimates may reﬂect uncertainties in activity data and emission factors, together with the limited representation of seasonal variability in bottom-up inventories. Furthermore, our best estimates of the total anthropogenic methane emissions for India and Bangladesh closely agree with satellite-based estimates reported by East et al. (22.3–26.7 Tg a⁻¹ and 4.8–5.2 Tg a⁻¹, respectively)40, although differencesremain in livestock and fossil-fuel emissions. In brief, differences between our estimates and previous top-down studies may reﬂect different setups in the inversion framework, study period, prior emission inventory used, and spatial resolution. We provide a more detailed comparison and discuss potential factors driving the differences in Text S3.

Interannual changes in methane emissions over South Asia, 2019–2024 Figure 4a shows the interannual variability (IAV) of posterior methane emissions over South Asia from 2019 to 2024. Total methane emissions show large IAV over the study period, with values of 34.6 Tg a⁻¹ (32.3–39.5 Tg a⁻1, uncertainty range from the inversion ensemble) in 2019, slightly decreasing to 34.3 (33.0–38.7) Tg a⁻¹ in 2020, followed by a sharp increase of ~16% in 2021, reaching 39.7 (38.8–42.4) Tg a⁻¹. Emissions remained at a similarly elevated level in 2022, before declining in 2023 and subsequently rebounding in 2024. The IAV of posterior sectoral attributions shows that methane emissionsacrossSouthAsiaarelargelygovernedbyanthropogenicsectorsrather than natural wetlands (Fig. 4b). In South Asia, anthropogenic sources account for 25.3–30.9 Tg a⁻¹ throughout the study period, substantially exceeding wetland emissions of 7.2–9.0 Tg a⁻¹. The IAV of anthropogenic emissions differs from that reported by Qu et al.35, who found that anthropogenic methane emissions over South Asia (India and Pakistan) increased from 2019 to 2020 and then declined in 2021. These differences likely reﬂect the overly large interannual changes in OH concentrations

simulatedinQuetal.35,whichcaninturnaffectmethaneemissionestimates. Their global coarse resolution (4o × 5o) may also introduce source aliasing72. In addition, unlike the separate dry- and wet-season inversions used here, Qu et al.35 performed annual-mean inversions, which again imposed seasonality from the prior knowledge (discussed in Text S4). Wetland emissions in our analysis increased by 1.5 and 1.8 Tg a⁻¹ in 2020 and 2021, respectively. This enhancement is consistent with Lin et al.16, who reported increases of 1.7 ± 4.1 and 4.5 ± 1.4 Tg a⁻¹ over the Ganges ﬂoodplain for the same years, and is supported by the observed liquid waterequivalent (LWE) trends from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment satellites (GRACE-FO)73 across South Asia in 2020–2021 relative to 2019. Figure 4c shows a detailed breakdown of major anthropogenic sectors, with dry- and wet-season variations shown in Fig. 2. Emissions from livestock, rice cultivation, and wastemanagement acrossSouth Asia alldeclined from 2019 to 2020, followed by a pronounced increase from 2021 onward, consistent with a reduction in human activities during the COVID-19 pandemic and a subsequent rebound. Similar declines in anthropogenic methane emissions during COVID-19 lockdowns have also been reported in previous studies8,74–76. Livestock emissions rose to 14.2 (14.0–14.9) Tg a⁻¹ in 2022, before decreasing in 2023 and increasing again in 2024, while rice and waste emissions follow similar trajectoriesbut peak earlier in 2021at 8.9 (8.8–9.1) Tg a⁻¹ and 5.8 (5.4–6.7) Tg a⁻¹, respectively. Wetland emissions, which are primarily controlled by climatic and hydrological conditions rather than direct human activity, show only weak year-to-year variations over this period (Fig. 4b). Figure 4d gives the IAV of methane emissions from the dry and wet seasons separately. We ﬁnd that dry-season emissions dominate the IAV, despite wet-season emissions dominating the overall magnitude. Year-toyear changes in total emissions more closely track those in the dry season than in the wet season, with a strong correlation of Δ total (Δ denotes yearto-year changes) with Δ dry-season emissions (r = 0.9), compared to a weaker relationship with Δ wet-season emissions (r = 0.2). Considering seasonal sectoral patterns (Fig. 2) and interannual changes (Fig. 4a), our ﬁndings suggest that dry-season anthropogenic emissions are likely the primary driver of IAV in South Asia, with livestock and waste being the dominantcontributors.Suchenhanceddry-seasonsensitivityisplausible,as emissions during this period are more strongly constrained by water and temperature availability, and waste/manure decomposition conditions77–79. Modest changes in precipitation deﬁcits, droughts, irrigation demand, or heat extremes may therefore substantially alter methane-producing conditions80. These ﬁndings suggest that dry-season emissions may be more sensitive to climate variability, with potential implications for designing more climate-resilient mitigation strategies.

Comparison with a global TROPOMI inversion by He et al. Figure 5 compares our emission results in South Asia with those obtained from a global inversion by He et al.42. He et al.42 conducted an annual-mean optimization, in which the seasonality is prescribed in the prior assumption and is not allowed to be optimized in the inversion. The year-to-year emission changes from 2019–2024 in our work generally agree with those reported by He et al.42, despite differing in annual magnitudes. For individual years, emissions estimated by He et al.42 exceed our uncertainty range for 2019–2021, but fall within it for 2022–2024. Overall, emissions reported by He et al.42 are on average 12.2% higher than our best estimate. To investigate this discrepancy, we conduct a test by carrying out an annual-mean regional inversion over the South Asia domain for 2019 (see Text S4 and Fig. S3) and ﬁnd that it also yields higher emissions (+17.5%) than our annual estimate (dry + wet periods) here. We discuss in detail in the supplemental on the sensitivity test and potential bias associated withan annual-meaninversionsetup;inbrief,such asetup canyieldover-orunderestimations of emissions due to boundary condition corrections in a regional inversion. These biases may propagate to affect the IAV estimate, and likely contribute to the discrepancies between our results and those of He et al.42. Furthermore, their global inversion was conducted at a much coarser spatial resolution (2° × 2.5° versus 0.25° × 0.3125° in our work), which may lead to spatial aliasing between South Asia and surrounding regions35.

Discussion Quantiﬁcation of methane emissions over South Asia during the wet season remains notoriously difﬁcult, as dense cloud cover limits satellite observations over the high-emitting regions. Here, we perform separate inversions for the dry and wet seasons, aiming to better account for the seasonal variabilityandimprovetheaccuracyoftheinversionestimates.Byincluding downwind observations that have the potential to capture signals transported from upwind source regions, we achieve a degree of freedom for signal (DOFS) in the wet season comparable to that in the dry season, despite much sparser observational coverage. Our results show that methane emissions in the wet season dominate the regional total in South Asia, nearly twice those in the dry season (compared on an annual basis). Speciﬁcally, emissions from rice cultivation, wetlands, waste management, and fossil fuels are higher in the wet season. Higher wet-season waste emissions are driven by enhanced microbial methanogenesis and altered handling under increased precipitation and runoff, consistent with the results derived from a global point source survey using the GHGSat satellite constellation65. Meanwhile, higher wet-season fossil fuel emissions likely reﬂect increased electricity demand for cooling. The IAV in methane emissions in South Asia is dominated by dry-season anthropogenic sectors, with livestock and waste being the largest contributors. The decline in anthropogenic emissions in 2020 and the subsequent rebound are consistent with changes in COVID-19-related human activity8,74–76. In particular, emissions from livestock manure and waste can vary with temperature and moisture conditions that inﬂuence microbial decomposition and methanogenesis78. Dry-season rice emissions may also be affected by anomalies in precipitation and water availability through changes in irrigation and ﬁeld inundation82. These climate-sensitive processes may provide plausible pathways through which dry-season hydroclimatic variability could contribute to year-to-year changes in regional methane emissions77,80. The role of South Asia in recent global methane surges differs largely from year to year. Although wetland emissions in South Asia increased in 2020 relative to 2019, total and anthropogenic methane emissions in the region declined during that year, in contrast to the contemporaneous global upward trend. This divergence indicates that South Asia was unlikely to have contributed to the global methane growth observed in 2020, which instead has been attributed to enhanced wetland emissions and changes in atmospheric sinks in recent studies8,16,50. By contrast, for the global surge in 2021, global anthropogenic methane emissions increased from 348.4 Tg a−1

in 2020 to 364.8 Tg a−1 in 202142. Over the same period, methane emissions inSouthAsiarosefrom25.3to30.3 Tg a⁻¹,accountingfor~30%oftheglobal increase. This is consistent with the ﬁndings of He et al.42 and Pendergrass etal.27.Thedifferingcontributionsof SouthAsiafromyeartoyearreﬂectthe complexity of the drivers underlying global methane growth, highlighting the need for detailed regional studies to better understand these processes. Our ﬁndings on the seasonal and interannual emission variations imply that while wet-season emissions (rice and waste in particular) are the primary targets for reducing total methane emissions, dry-season anthropogenic emissions play a critical role in shaping variability and uncertainty, requiring adaptive and climate-resilient mitigation strategies. Resolving seasonal source variability in South Asia can therefore improve attribution of recent global methane growth and reduce uncertainty in global methane budget assessments. The seasonal constraints can also inform mitigation by identifying key contributing sectors and periods when mitigation may be most effective.

Methods TROPOMI satellite observations We usetheTROPOMIXCH4 product fortheinversioncoveringNovember 2018 to October 2024. TROPOMI observations are from the blended TROPOMI + GOSAT product of Balasus et al.34 and corrected for systematic artifacts using collocated GOSAT observations through a machine-

learning approach. Only high-quality retrievals with a quality assurance value greater than 0.5 are used. We further exclude full-water pixels (surface_classiﬁcation = 1)andcoastalpixelsinﬂuencedbypartialwatersurfaces (surface_classiﬁcation = 3). TROPOMI data are unavailable from 26 July to 23August2022, from 10to 30August2023 (with retrievalqualitydegrading from26Julyonward),andfrom29Mayto3June,11to18July,26to31July, and 26 to 29 September 2024, owing to missing VIIRS cloud data. The number of successful TROPOMI retrievals used by the inversion for each season during 2019–2024 is summarized in Table S4. Persistent cloud cover and sparse surface observations during the South Asian wet seasons (Fig. S12) substantially reduce the availability and representativeness of atmospheric measurements, limiting our ability to quantify regional methane emissions. In this study, following the regionalscale downwind framework of Xu et al.44, we constrain methane emissions over South Asia by exploiting large-scale downwind transport signals captured by satellite observations. This approach integrates information over broad spatial scales, allowing robust emission constraints even when local observations are sparse during the wet seasons. Details of the method are provided in the Supplementary Information (Text S1).

Prior estimates Fig. S6 shows prior methane emissions by sector in South Asia. Emissions from wastewater, landﬁlls, and other anthropogenic sectors are taken from EDGAR v847. Livestock emissions are from EDGAR v748, owing to pronounced spatial hotspots and the absence of explicit seasonal variability in the livestock sector of EDGAR v8. Rice cultivation emissions are based on the Global Rice Paddy Inventory (GRPI)22. Emissions from coal and oil/gas exploitation (including offshore activities) are taken from the Global Fuel ExploitationInventory(GFEIv3)49.Wetlandemissionsarederivedfromthe Lund-Potsdam-Jena Earth Observation Simulator (LPJ-EOSIM) dynamic global vegetation model, driven by MERRA-2 meteorology50. Biomass burning emissions are from GFED483, termite emissions are from Fung et al.84, and geological seepage emissions are from Etiope et al.85. For years not covered bya giveninventory,emissionsare assumed to be equaltothose of the nearest available year.

GEOS-Chem forward model TheGEOS-Chemchemicaltransportmodel(version13.0.0; https://doi.org/ 10.5281/zenodo.4618180, last accessed: June 2026) is used as the forward model in the inversion to connect methane emissions with atmospheric observations. The GEOS-Chem model is driven by GEOS-FP meteorological ﬁelds from the NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Ofﬁce86, with spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.3125° and temporal resolution of 3 h. Methane sinks from atmospheric oxidation and soil uptake are included in the global simulation, but are inconsequential in the nested domain because the regional ventilation timescale is much shorter than the atmospheric lifetime of methane38,39,87. To enable direct comparison with TROPOMI observations, simulated vertical proﬁles of methane dry mixing ratios are convolved with the TROPOMI averaging kernel vectors and corresponding prior vertical proﬁles88, yielding model-consistent XCH4 ﬁelds. Boundary and initial conditions (deﬁnedas the ﬁrst day of each season) are taken from a global GEOS-Chem simulation that has been bias-corrected to match TROPOMI XCH4

87. In addition, boundary conditions along the northern, southern, western, and eastern edges of the regional domain are optimized separately for each season within the inversion framework (Table S4).

Analytical inversion Following our previous work38,39, we apply the Gaussian mixture model (GMM)51 to construct the emission state vector x for seasonal inversions over November 2018–October 2024. Following the South Asian monsoon cycle, each year is divided into a dry (November–May) and wet (June–October) season to explicitly resolve monsoon-driven variability, yielding 12 inversions in total. The GMM retains ﬁne spatial detail in strong source regions while consolidating weaker sources according to the prior emission distribution. Guided by prior information-content analyses, we

We use error correlations between posterior national emission estimates (0: perfect separation; ±1: no separation) to assess the ability of the inversion to distinguish emissions from individual countries (Figs. S4 and S5). The inversion can separate major emission sectors, except for landﬁlls and wastewater treatment, which are combined into a single waste category in this study91.

Inversion ensemble and uncertainty estimate To better characterize uncertainty in the posterior estimates, we perform an ensemble of sensitivity inversions for each seasonal inversion and quantify the posterior uncertainty as the spread of solutions across the inversion ensemble39. The ensemble explores uncertainties associated with the prior emission error standard deviation and the regularization parameter γ. Speciﬁcally, the prior emission error standard deviation is prescribed at three levels (25%, 50%, and 75%), while γ is varied by ±50% around its optimal value determined following the criterion of Lu et al.37. This design yields 108 sensitivity inversions, comprising 9 sensitivity inversions for each of 12 inversion periods (2 seasons × 6 years), which are used to quantify the robustness and uncertainty of the inferred methane emissions. The interannual range is deﬁned by the minimum and maximum annual best estimates for 2019 to 2024, whereas the inversion uncertainty is deﬁned by the envelope of estimates across the sensitivity inversion ensemble.
